mappings.note: A one-line definition of conservation of mass in terms of reactants and products. Statement only, so LO-48. The chapter's explain-and-illustrate version (286c6b21) and its bench-verification versions (b7965e32, 9c466b2f) sit on LO-40 and LO-39 respectively.
State the law of constant proportions and attribute it to Proust. Familiarity-level statement of LO-48's 'elements combine in fixed ratios form compounds'.

Recall of the 1:8 hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio in water. The canonical instance of the fixed-ratio concept, LO-48 - no reasoning, no arithmetic, no source comparison (which is what pushes 6880d5a5 to LO-40).

Asks for the law's significance, i.e. what follows from it for chemistry as a whole. That is explanation, LO-40, and it is what separates this item from the neighbouring ff3f705b, which only asks the student to state the same law.
Produce a second instance of the law (CO2 at 3:8) rather than repeating the textbook's water example. Instantiating a law is explaining it, LO-40; the bare statement of the same law is LO-48.

What an atom is according to Dalton. Dalton is named only in LO-40, so it takes every postulate item; LO-48's 'matter are made of particles' is the un-attributed version of the same idea and is used for items that do not invoke the theory.

The Dalton postulate that atoms of one element are identical and atoms of different elements differ. LO-40 for the attribution. Not LO-39: its differentiation list covers atoms against molecules and elements against compounds, not one element's atoms against another's.
How Dalton's theory explains constant proportions - the simple whole-number ratio postulate. Both halves of the item are named in LO-40's own text, which is why no second code is added.

What causes a covalent bond to form: sharing of valence pairs for stability. Formation, LO-40. Its definition-only sibling c91b4c01 (ionic bond) is mapped to LO-48 because it asks what the bond IS, not what brings it about.

Describe O2's bonding: two shared pairs, one double bond. Mechanism, LO-40 - the same outcome as the O2 drawing and sequencing items, honestly shared, since the frame has one covalent-formation outcome.
Correct a false claim about how nitrogen trichloride is named. A nomenclature convention item, LO-42; the metal/non-metal error in the stem is incidental to the naming rule being corrected.

Why a chlorine atom must share an electron with another chlorine atom. The driver for covalent formation, LO-40. The octet reasoning here has no outcome of its own in this frame - it appears only inside competency C1.1's text.

How a sodium cation differs from a neutral sodium atom in electron count. Telling a cation from its parent atom is LO-39's 'cations and anions' differentiation clause; LO-41 would apply if the item asked the student to work the charge out rather than state the difference.

The term for the oppositely charged species formed by gain or loss of electrons, with cation and anion named against each other. LO-39's cation/anion clause; no charge is calculated, so LO-41 stays out.

A textbook definition of the ionic bond. Naming a type of bonding at familiarity level, LO-48, and deliberately not LO-40: the neighbouring item 53361729 asks what causes a covalent bond to form, which is the formation outcome, while this one asks only what the bond is.

The structure ionic bonding produces - six chloride neighbours around every sodium in the lattice. Mapped to LO-40 as the product of ionic formation. Where a lattice item instead contrasts an ionic solid with discrete molecules (1f71e06b) the code is LO-39.
The general rule for a binary formula: symbols, then crossover of valencies. LO-42's method clause, expressed generically rather than applied to a compound.

Aluminium sulfate by criss-cross. Shares LO-42 with every other formula item in the chapter, which is the honest position - LO-42 is the frame's only formula-writing outcome and nothing below it splits polyatomic from monatomic anions.
Why brackets are needed in Mg(OH)2. A convention explanation, LO-42; the aluminium hydroxide version (e397cce8) is the same demand on a different compound.
CCl4 from valencies 4 and 1. LO-42 again; the compound is covalent but the crossover convention and the outcome are unchanged, since LO-42 says 'simple compounds' without restriction.
One stated difference in water solubility between ionic and covalent compounds. Textbook LO-39: two named compound classes separated by a property.
Why solid sodium chloride cannot conduct. Property-based characterisation, LO-39 - the same outcome as its MCQ twin 9d6814a5 and, as there, a slightly loose fit because only one species is in play.

Under what condition an ionic compound does conduct: molten or dissolved. The complementary half of the conductivity property, still LO-39; together with 53644a5f it forms the contrast the outcome actually describes.

The general link between bond type and melting point. This is the differentiation stated as a rule rather than applied, but the outcome is the same LO-39 - the frame has no separate 'generalise a property trend' outcome.

Define molecular mass. LO-41 is the only outcome that names molecular mass as such, and defining it is the front half of calculating it. LO-39 would be right only if the item set molecular mass against formula unit mass, which is what 05734bfa and 071cc2b7 do.
